newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt mkts end weaker, start to look good buying.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt mkts end weaker, start to look good buying.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against yesterday's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (MAR) 92.26 (PREV 92.35) 90-DAYS 7.70 (PREV 7.63)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.30 PCT (PREV 7.20) US 5-YR 6.35 (PREV 6.19)
* NZ bonds end weaker but off lows after Greenspan comments
* 2001 bond tender goes reasonably well
* Bear tone prevails but prices starting to look attractive

New Zealand bonds closed weaker on Thursday but off their intra-session lows, with dealers saying they had held up reasonably well after the sell-off triggered by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments overnight.

In his testimony before a Senate committee, Greenspan gave upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy but voiced concern about soaring stock prices and the risk of higher inflation. U.S. stock and bond prices tumbled on the remarks, and New Zealand bonds followed suit, with most maturities opening about 14 points weaker.
But dealers said insitutions had taken advantage of the lower prices.
"It's been solid sort of business. We've seen buying support in the early 7.60 percent area as the institutions make pretty much their first purchases for the whole month," said one.
He added that the NZ$100 million 2001 bond tender, which was fully subscribed and produced an average yield of 7.640 percent, had gone well given the magnitude of the move overnight.
The 01s closed at 7.58 percent.

At present prices, New Zealand bonds represented good value, but the bear run was not necessarily over yet and a break of 7.70 percent in the 06s would signal a resumption of the bear trend in earnest, dealers said.
In the money market, bills had also started to look attractive after weakening on Greenspan's comments, but trade was subdued.
"We saw a very small covering rally prior to lunch, mainly led in the futures, and this afternoon it's really just drifted off a little bit again on the back of the TWI weakening," said a trader.
"But the short rates really do seem pretty cheap for investors."
He said the short end would probably now trade a 7.55-7.75 percent range, providing the TWI did not weaken substantially, "and there probably is a reasonable chance it could".

"Things are probably still going to remain bearish for the remainder of the week and maybe into next week, but there's going to be a point where they're pretty good value -- 7.75 percent in the 90-days is probably going to start becoming pretty attractive," he said.
Dealers said there had been some manipulation of the cash market this session.

"There's a little bit of a play going on in the cash market. One name has been going in and bidding up cash to try and force all the short-dated stuff up. They haven't been very successful so far," said one, adding that it would be interesting to see whether the "name" persisted in the same vein on Friday.
The cash rate ended at 7.30 percent, up from 7.20 percent.
